author: BrentDesk Staff
headline: The attendance figure reported from AIM Congress belongs to last year's event
deck: A number carried as this year's result matches the 2025 edition exactly, which is a warning about how event statistics travel.
excerpt: An attendance figure widely reported from AIM Congress 2026 matches the 2025 edition's published result precisely, illustrating how event statistics are recycled.
content:
AIM Congress closed its fifteenth edition at Dubai World Trade Centre on 9 September, and the attendance figure attached to it in coverage requires a caution.

The number reported was 15,831 participants from 181 countries, with 1,385 speakers across 431 sessions. Those figures match the published result of the 2025 edition exactly — the same participant count to the individual delegate, the same country count. The 2026 pre-show material, by contrast, claimed more than 20,000 participants and over 400 institutions.

Two numbers cannot both be this year's. A figure identical to last year's to the digit is last year's figure, carried forward into coverage of the current event.

This is not necessarily anyone's deliberate misrepresentation, and it is worth explaining because the mechanism recurs. Event organisers publish audited results some weeks after a show closes. Those results then sit in press material, on websites and in search indexes, and are picked up when the next edition is written about — particularly by outlets working to a deadline on an event that has not yet released its own count. Nobody checks the year attached to the number because the number looks plausible.

The same pattern appeared elsewhere in this month's Gulf calendar. The International Property Show, which closed on the same day, has one outlet reporting 35,000 participants from 190 countries, an organiser projection of well over 30,000, and an audited 2025 result of 30,719 from 153 countries. Three figures, one of them audited and none of them this year's confirmed count.

The consequence for anyone using these numbers commercially is real. Exhibitors evaluate shows on attendance, sponsors price against it, and organisers sell space on it. A figure carried forward from a prior edition flatters or misrepresents an event's current draw, and it is the kind of error that compounds as each year's coverage cites the last.

The reliable approach is narrow: use figures the organiser has published for the specific edition, describe projections as projections, and wait for audited results rather than reporting a number that appeared during the show. Where an organiser has not published a count, saying so is more useful than repeating one from elsewhere.

AIM's substantive material this year was in its Africa sessions, where the UAE's $110bn of investment into African projects between 2019 and 2023 and Ethiopia's stated 60,000 megawatt renewable potential were both put on the record. Those figures have identifiable sources and dates attached, which is what makes them usable.

No closing communiqué or audited attendance count had been published as this edition closed.
